translation_en:
Yue Xuan 樂選 was registered in a civilian household in Wanping County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a native of Renhe County, Zhejiang. A prefectural school student, he specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Shunju; he ranked second in birth order and was twenty-eight years old, born on the eighteenth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Ashan, his grandfather Chun, his father Benhao, and his mother née Zhang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brother was Dao and his younger brother Da. He married a woman née Liu. He placed nineteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Guang 陳洸 was registered in a civilian household in Chaoyang County, Chaozhou Prefecture, Guangdong. A county school student, he specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Shijie; he ranked fourteenth in birth order and was thirty-three years old, born on the twelfth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Shilong, his grandfather Yongyin, his father Changyan〔an Imperial University student〕, and his mother née Zhuang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Xida, Wang, Jiang〔a tribute scholar〕, and Ying; his younger brothers were Wei and Ze. He married a woman née Wu and subsequently a woman née Zheng. He placed fifty-fourth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lü Zhe 呂悊 was registered in a civilian household in Yongfeng County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Wenchuan; he ranked second in birth order and was twenty-six years old, born on the second day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Ji, his grandfather Ce〔a Judge promoted to Investigating Censor〕, and his father Shi〔Vice Commissioner of a Provincial Surveillance Commission, advanced to the prestige title Yazhong dafu〕. His mother was née Guan〔posthumously awarded the title Lady of Respect〕, and his birth mother was née Deng〔awarded the title Lady for Attendance〕. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Hao, Huai〔Instructor in a medical school〕, and Lan. He married a woman née Yu. He placed seventy-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 267th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Wan 王完 was registered in a civilian household in Tongchuan Subprefecture, Sichuan, and was a native of Suining County. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Shudao; he ranked first in birth order and was twenty-one years old, born on the third day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Wenpu, his grandfather Chan〔Gentleman of Literary Distinction〕, his father Shao〔a titular official〕, and his mother née Cheng. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Qi, Xuan, Jun〔an Imperial University student〕, and Kai; his younger brothers were Hong, Cai, Ning〔a metropolitan graduate (jinshi)〕, Jin, Yu, Chen, and Yu. He married a woman née He. He placed sixtieth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and one hundredth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Yu Ji 俞集, courtesy name Rucheng, was registered in a civilian household in Xinchang County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. A National University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked second in his family and was thirty years old, born on the tenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather Shumei was granted the title of Secretary in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice; his grandfather Duo was Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud, advanced to the prestige title Grand Master of the Second Rank (Yazhong dafu). His father was Pu, and his mother was née Lü; both parents were living. His elder brother’s name is illegible (□); the text concerning his younger brother or brothers is unclear (□□行□□) [?]. His wife was née Lü. He placed eighty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred eighty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhan Chong 詹崇, courtesy name Donglu, was registered in a civilian household in Le’an County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. A National University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked ninth in his family and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twelfth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yishan, his grandfather Qitai, and his father Zunxun; his mother was née You, and his stepmother was née Zhu. His father alone was living. His elder brother was Chang; the name or names of his younger brother or brothers are illegible (□□). His wife was née Pan. He placed ninetieth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred thirty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Bi Lian 畢濂, courtesy name Jingzhou, was registered in a civilian household in Guixi County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi. A National University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked thirty-first in his family and was thirty-one years old, born on the eighteenth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Huai’an, his grandfather Yuzhang, and his father Zhenyi; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Zhen, and his younger brother was Luo. He married a woman née Xu and was subsequently betrothed to a woman née Wang. He placed twelfth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and one hundred thirtieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zang Xiang 臧相, courtesy name Zuoliang, was registered in an official household at Jiantiao Battalion, Taizhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a native of Ninghai County. A National University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked eighth in his family and was thirty-two years old, born on the twentieth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather Canggai was an Assistant Commander, and his grandfather Lisheng was a Vice Chiliarch. His father was Hai, and his mother was née Li; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Sen, Lun, Ke (a Chiliarch), Zhu, and Yi; his younger brothers were Tang, Bin, Nan, Kai, Yu, Huai, and Qiao. His wife was née Yu. He placed forty-ninth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and twenty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Dong Jiao 東郊 was registered in a civilian household in Huazhou, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, and was a student of the subprefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Xisong. Fourth in birth order, he was thirty-two years old, born on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Ji; his grandfather, Sheng, was a County Vice Magistrate, posthumously granted the title of Director in the Ministry of Justice; his father, Sizhong, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner; and his mother, née Xue, held the title Lady of Suitability. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Zhou, an honorary official; Lu, a Prefectural Judge; and □, a tribute scholar. His younger brothers were Ye, a Secretary in the Ministry of Justice, and Shi. He married a woman née Zhang and subsequently a woman née Dou. He placed fifty-fourth [?] in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 115th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Mengxiong 劉夢熊 was registered in a civilian household in Wenshang County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Poetry; his courtesy name was Boxiang. First in birth order, he was twenty-four years old, born on the twenty-seventh day of the eighth month. The great-grandfather’s entry is illegible [?]; his grandfather was Xi, an honorary official; his father, Yi, was a County Magistrate; and his mother was née Wang. His parents’ survival status is illegible [?]. His younger brothers were Zhongxiang, an Instructor in the School of Yin and Yang, and Meng□□, a student of the Imperial University. He married a woman née Hu and subsequently a woman née Wang. His rank in the Shandong Provincial Examination is partly illegible: 三□□□ [?]. He placed 181st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ji Tai 吉泰 was registered in a civilian household in Linqing Subprefecture, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong, and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Shangxian. First in birth order, he was twenty-nine years old, born on the third day of the second month. The great-grandfather’s entry is illegible [?]; his grandfather was Ying, his father was Rong, and his mother was née Zhuang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Guoguang. He married a woman née Wang. He placed eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 306th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Maode 鄭懋德 was registered in a civilian household in Putian County, □□ Prefecture, Fujian, and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Chengzhao. He was apparently second in birth order and thirty years old [the intervening text is illegible, ?], born on the second day of the intercalary eighth month. His great-grandfather, Dao, was a County Magistrate; his grandfather was Kongyong; his father, Ke, was a sacrificial official; his mother was née Wang, and his stepmother was née Xu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Mao’ang and Maoxian; his younger brothers were Maoxun and Maohe. He married a woman née Chen. He placed thirty-fourth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 172nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Hanqing 張漢卿 was registered in Yifeng County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Yuanjie, and he ranked first among his brothers. He was thirty years old, born on the seventh day of the intercalary eighth month. His great-grandfather was Jin; his grandfather, Duan, was a Police Chief; his father, Ying, was a District Magistrate; and his mother was née Li. His mother alone survived. He married a woman née Wu. He placed forty-eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 310th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jin Xuan 金選 was registered in Jingmen Subprefecture, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang, in a civilian household, and was originally from Fengcheng County, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Weixian, and he ranked third among his brothers. He was forty years old, born on the fifth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather’s name is partly illegible, ending in Zhen [?]; his grandfather was Dehou; his father was Zhang; his mother was née Hu, and his stepmother was née Chen. The statement of his parents’ survival is illegible [?]. His elder brothers were Lan and Shi, and his younger brothers were Guan, Shan, Yuan, and Duo. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently a woman née Li. He placed sixteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination [?] and 298th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Zhang 孫漳 was registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. He was Instructor at the county school of Nanling, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Xixue, and he ranked twentieth among his brothers. He was thirty-nine years old, born on the twenty-first day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather’s name is partly illegible, ending in Sheng [?]; his grandfather was Shangzhen; his father was E; and his mother was née Zhang. His father alone survived. His younger brothers were Jing and Wei. He married a woman née Zhou. He placed third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and fifty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cheng Peng 程鵬 was registered in Jie Subprefecture, in a prefecture whose surviving name ends in Yang, in a province whose surviving name begins with Shan [?], in a civilian household. A student of the Directorate of Education, he specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was □wan, and he ranked first among his brothers. He was thirty-five years old, born on the twenty-seventh day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Xing; his grandfather was Jing; his father was Gang; and his mother was née Tan. Both parents survived. His younger brother was E. He married a woman née Chang. He placed fifty-second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 283rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Aoshan, courtesy name Ruli, was registered in a civilian household in Anfu County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. A county school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked second among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the twentieth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather Hong was an Investigating Censor, posthumously granted the title of Right Censor-in-Chief of the Nanjing Censorate [?]; his grandfather Fuhua was Left Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate; his father Wei held honorary official status; and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Wushan, and his younger brothers were Nanshan, Jiushan, Chushan, Shunshan, Chunshan, and Qingshan. His wife was née Ouyang. He placed fiftieth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 290th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Song Chen, courtesy name Yizhong, was registered in a military household in Huating County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first among his brothers and was forty-two years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the third month. His great-grandfather's name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Jie, his father Jin, and his mother née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His younger brother was Xiang, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed thirty-eighth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eightieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zun, courtesy name Zhongyi, was registered in a civilian household in Tongchuan Subprefecture, Sichuan, and was a native of Suining County. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the twelfth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Xuan; his grandfather Yu held the prestige title Gentleman of Literature; and his father Shaoji held a seventh-rank prestige title. His father's former wife was née Fang, and his mother was née Chen. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Gong, Xuan, Mi, You (a tribute scholar), Shi, Wan (a metropolitan graduate of the same examination year), Hong, and Cai; his younger brothers were Zai, Yu, Chen, and Yu. His wife was née Yang. He placed second in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and thirty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Kai, courtesy name Ziwan, was registered in a civilian household in Dao Subprefecture, Yongzhou Prefecture, Huguang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked eighth among his brothers and was thirty-six years old, born on the fourth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Jing, his grandfather Kongxuan, his father Wenhao, and his mother née Wen. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Rui, Ming, and Quan, and his younger brother was Zhao. His wife was née Li. He placed fifty-fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 231st in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
He Bangxian, of civilian registration in Taihe County, Dali Prefecture, Yunnan, was an additional student at the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zongyin; he ranked first among his brothers, was aged thirty-six, and was born on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Shan, his grandfather Xian, his father Zhen, and his mother née Yang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brothers were Bangzan, Bangjian, Bangxiu, Bangjun, Bangzhi, Bangfan, and Bangru. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently a woman née Su. He placed twenty-sixth in the Yunnan–Guizhou Provincial Examination and 346th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Dai Xiang, of civilian registration in Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili, was a county-school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yinghe; he ranked first among his brothers, was aged forty-seven, and was born on the eighteenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□□); his grandfather was Zicheng, his father Liu, a County Magistrate, and his mother née Ge. His parents’ survival status is illegible (□□下) [?]. His younger brother was Rui. He married a woman née Hu. He placed forty-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

□□Shi (□□示; name uncertain [?]), of military registration in Anlu Guard, Huguang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Pingfu; he ranked second among his brothers, was aged thirty-eight, and was born on the thirtieth day of the intercalary sixth month. His great-grandfather, whose name is illegible (□□), was posthumously granted the title of Right Censor-in-Chief at Nanjing. His grandfather Cong was granted the title of Right Assistant Censor-in-Chief and posthumously granted that of Right Censor-in-Chief of the Nanjing Censorate. His father Hong was Right Censor-in-Chief of the Nanjing Censorate; his mother, née Tang, was granted the title of Lady. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Cai; his younger brothers were Gai, a tribute scholar, Qu, and Nie, a tribute scholar. He married a woman née Gao. He placed sixth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 116th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Peng Yingzhen, of civilian registration in Xian County, Hejian Prefecture, Zhili, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Dezheng; he ranked second among his brothers, was aged thirty-three, and was born on the first day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Shijing, his grandfather Zhao, an Investigating Censor, his father Mao, a County Magistrate, and his mother née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yingkui; his younger brothers were Yingshen and Yingmao. He married a woman née Chen and subsequently a woman née Liu. He placed eighty-ninth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 150th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Juren 張居仁, courtesy name Gongfu, was registered in a civilian household in Jingzhou, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-seven, and born on the seventeenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Duo; his grandfather, Youxin; his father, Yong, a District Magistrate; and his mother, née Wang. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Juyi, Juli, Jushan, Juzhi, Juxing, and Jude. His wife was née Gu. He ranked eightieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 158th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Hu Qiong 胡瓊, courtesy name Guohua, was registered in a civilian household in Nanping County, Yanping Prefecture, Fujian. A prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the twentieth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□□); his grandfather was Zhuang; and his father, Shengchang. His legal mother was née Wang, and his birth mother was née Zhang. His parents’ survival status is illegible (□□下) [?]. His younger brothers were Gong and Xuan. His wife was née Jin. He ranked fiftieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and forty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

The candidate’s name is illegible (□□□). His courtesy name was Lizhi. He was registered in an artisan household under the Embroidered-Uniform Guard and was a native of Jiaxing County, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-five, and born on the seventeenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Ji; his father, Wan; his mother, née Li; and his successive stepmothers, née Xu and née Chen. Both parents were deceased. The following family information is illegible (□□□) [?]. His wife was née Cui; he subsequently married a woman née Wu. He ranked 117th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and ninetieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mao Zhen 毛震, courtesy name Qizhi, was registered in a civilian household in Kunshan County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged forty-one, and born on the sixth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenxian; his grandfather, Ji; and his father’s name is illegible (□□). His mother was née Li, and his stepmother was née Jin. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His wife was née Yan. He ranked 121st in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 245th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wan Chao 萬潮, registered in a civilian household in Jinxian County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Ruxin, and he ranked tenth among his brothers and male cousins. He was twenty-four, born on the twenty-fifth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather Yuanhe was a Professor, posthumously granted the title of Assistant Prefect; his grandfather Fu was a Registrar; and his father Kai was a District Magistrate. His mother was née Wu, and his stepmother née Hu. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Jin, and his younger brothers were Lan, Pu, Shu, and Yu. He married a woman née Xu. He placed eighty-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Dun 俞敦, registered in an official household of Yangzhou Guard in the Metropolitan Region, was a student of the Jiangdu County school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Chongli, and he ranked eighth among his brothers and male cousins. He was thirty, born on the first day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was You; his grandfather Yonggui was a Company Commander; and his father Jun was a Vice Commissioner of the Hongxi Office [?]. His father's former wife, née Cui, had been granted the title of Lady; his mother was née Cheng. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Qing, a Company Commander; Min, a Vice Commander; Zheng and Chang, honorary officials; and Min 旼 and Xiao 敩, students of the Imperial University. His younger brothers were Mu, an honorary official, and Jing. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed 116th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 282nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Jiyuan 李際元, registered in a civilian household in Yanggu County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, was an added-quota student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Tongfu, and he ranked fifth among his brothers and male cousins. He was twenty-two, born on the sixteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather's name is illegible; his grandfather Xuan held a prestige title; and his father was Zizhang. His mother was née Shen. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yingyuan, and his younger brothers were Fuyuan, Jiyuan, and Zongyuan. He married a woman née Chen. His placing in the Shandong Provincial Examination is partly illegible: □□20 [?]; he placed 294th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jian Zuo 簡佐, registered in a civilian household in Xinyu County, Linjiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name is illegible, and he ranked sixth among his brothers and male cousins. His age is recorded as forty followed by an illegible character [?]; he was born on the seventeenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Dijian, his grandfather Zhenheng, and his father Xiangbin. His mother was née Qian. Both parents were deceased. He married a woman née Fu and subsequently a woman née Liu. He placed ninety-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 277th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
He Huang 何炾, registered in an artisan household in Jiangxia County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Mingshi; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-two, born on the seventh day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Yuanshan, his grandfather Rongzhou, and his father Dayi; his legal mother was née Li and his birth mother née Ma. His father was deceased and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Kai and □ [name illegible]. He married a woman née Pan and subsequently a woman née Xu. He placed fourteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 233rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Jie 鄭傑, registered in a military household of Xiangyang Guard, Huguang, and a native of Guangji County, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Boxing; he ranked fourth among his brothers and was aged forty-three, born on the third day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□□); his grandfather was Da and his father Yi. His father’s former wife was née Ma, his mother née Yang, and his stepmother also née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Ji, Lun, and Yi. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed third in the Huguang Provincial Examination and sixty-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Dezhen 施德禎, registered in a civilian household in Yuhang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Tianrui; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged twenty-seven, born on the eleventh day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Lun, his father Yue, and his mother née Wu. His father was deceased and his mother was living. His younger brothers were Defu, Deyou, Deyu, Dezhi, Depao, and Dexi. He married a woman née Wu. He placed seventy-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 206th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Zhi 路直, registered in a medical household in Luoyang County, Henan Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Jingfu; he ranked first among his brothers and was aged forty-two, born on the first day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Zongmao; his grandfather Tong was a county Registrar, and his father Jiu was a prefectural Clerk. His mother was née Wu and his stepmother née Li. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Fang, a student of the Imperial University, Ping, and Zheng. He married a woman née Sun. He placed eighth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 137th in the Metropolitan Examination.

His courtesy name was Zongqi; he ranked sixteenth in birth order and was aged forty-three, born on the eighth day of the twelfth month. He placed seventy-ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and two hundred fourteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Maowen 周懋文 was registered in a civilian household in Kunshan County, Suzhou Prefecture, Zhili, and was a county government school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Cunzhi; he ranked first in birth order and was aged thirty-three, born on the fifteenth day of the intercalary sixth month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Ang and his father Chuan; his mother was née Xiang. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Shangwen, and his wife was née Shen. He placed one hundred seventieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and one hundred eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

□□ [name illegible] was registered in a civilian household in Yuhang County, Hangzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Wancheng; he ranked sixth in birth order and was aged thirty-eight, born on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Xin, his grandfather Rang, and his father Xiang; his mother was née Lang. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Shan, Wen, Sheng 〔Guosuo [?]〕, Nan, Kang, Yin, and Qian [division of names uncertain]; his younger brother was Yi. His wife was née Shen, and his subsequent wife was also née Shen. He placed one hundred twenty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Xian 陳憲 was registered in a military household in Yugan County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Bodu; he ranked second in birth order and was aged forty-four, born on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Xihong, his grandfather Yitai, and his father Yongkuan; his mother was née Xu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yuanheng and Yuanli, and his wife was née Wu. He placed thirteenth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and one hundred forty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

蔣益，貫直隸常州府武進縣，軍籍，治禮記，字守謙，行四，年二十九，十一月二十六日生，縣學生。曾祖繼祖，祖能，父容〔知州〕，前母吳氏、單氏，母吉氏。具慶下。兄盤〔陰陽正術〕、孟〔義官〕、簠、簋；弟聸、監、璡、珀、珊、瓛〔貢士〕、纓。娶毛氏。應天府鄉試第一百□□名，會試第一百五十四名。

張學禮，貫直隸順德府平鄉縣，民籍，治春秋，字以立，行一，年二十四，閏正月初六日生，國子生。曾祖□□，祖德林，父欽，母蘭氏，繼母郭氏。□□下。兄學詩。娶焦氏。□□鄉試第八十四名，會試第一百三十九名。

□□輔，貫山西汾州平遙縣，軍籍，治易經，字廷章，行二，年四十三，十二月二十二日生，國子生。曾祖□，祖守道，父鑑，母李氏，繼母侯氏。具慶下。兄宣；弟黻。娶王氏，繼娶李氏、張氏。山西鄉試第六十四名，會試第二百三十三名。

康浩，貫陝西西安府乾州武功縣，民籍，治詩經，字德充，行七，年三十三，五月十九日生，國子生。曾祖爵〔太常寺卿〕，祖健〔通政司知事〕，父鑾〔金吾右衛經歷〕，母高氏，繼母高氏。慈侍下。兄阜、淮、浤、澤〔醫學訓科〕、海、□、瀾；弟瀚、淳、洋、河、漁。娶魏氏。陝西鄉試第十三名，會試第三十九名。
translation_en:
Jiang Yi 蔣益 was registered in Wujin County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a military household. A county school student specializing in the Book of Rites, he had the courtesy name Shouqian, was fourth in birth order, and was aged twenty-nine, born on the twenty-sixth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Jizu; his grandfather, Neng; and his father, Rong 〔Department Magistrate〕. His father’s former wives were née Wu and née Shan; his mother was née Ji. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Pan 〔Yin-yang Specialist〕, Meng 〔Honorary Official〕, Fu, and Gui; his younger brothers were Dan, Jian, Jin, Po, Shan, Huan 〔tribute scholar〕, and Ying. His wife was née Mao. He placed 1□□ in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 154th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Xueli 張學禮 was registered in Pingxiang County, Shunde Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Yili, was first in birth order, and was aged twenty-four, born on the sixth day of the intercalary first month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□□); his grandfather was Delin; and his father, Qin. His mother was née Lan, and his stepmother was née Guo. His parental status is illegible (□□) [?]. His elder brother was Xueshi. His wife was née Jiao. He placed 84th in the Provincial Examination for an illegible jurisdiction (□□) and 139th in the Metropolitan Examination.

□□fu □□輔 was registered in Pingyao County, Fenzhou, Shanxi, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he had the courtesy name Tingzhang, was second in birth order, and was aged forty-three, born on the twenty-second day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather’s name is illegible (□); his grandfather was Shoudao; and his father, Jian. His mother was née Li, and his stepmother was née Hou. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Xuan, and his younger brother was Fu. His wife was née Wang; his subsequent wives were née Li and née Zhang. He placed 64th in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 233rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Kang Hao 康浩 was registered in Wugong County, Qianzhou, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he had the courtesy name Dechong, was seventh in birth order, and was aged thirty-three, born on the nineteenth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather was Jue 〔Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices〕; his grandfather, Jian 〔Clerk in the Office of Transmission〕; and his father, Luan 〔Registrar of the Right Jinwu Guard〕. His mother and stepmother were both née Gao. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Fu, Huai, Hong, Ze 〔Medical Instructor〕, Hai, one whose name is illegible (□), and Lan; his younger brothers were Han, Chun, Yang, He, and Yu. His wife was née Wei. He placed 13th in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 39th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhang Lu 張錄, courtesy name Zongzhi, was from a civilian household registered in Chengwu County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-fifth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yan, his grandfather Jing, and his father Cong; his father's principal wife was née Zhu, and his birth mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Xi and Quan, and his younger brothers Gao and Sui. He married a woman née Guo. He ranked thirty-eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 244th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chu Xun 儲洵, courtesy name Pingfu, was from a civilian household registered in Taizhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, Zhili. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-eight, and born on the twenty-first day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather, whose name is illegible (□), was posthumously granted the title of Right Vice Minister of Revenue; his grandfather Xin was granted the same title. His father was Lan, and his mother was née Fan. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xun [?—the same name as the candidate in the transcription], Yi, and Bo. He married a woman née Wang and subsequently another woman née Wang. He ranked seventy-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ji Jieyi 紀節義, courtesy name Dezhou, was from a civilian household registered in Chiping County, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the thirtieth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Liang, his grandfather Xuan, and his father Xian, a District Magistrate; his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Jieyong. He married a woman née Xue. He ranked first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and thirty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zun 王遵, courtesy name Shundian, was from a civilian household registered in Xuancheng County, Ningguo Prefecture, Zhili. A prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was sixth in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the nineteenth day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yunzhong, a Secretariat Drafter; his grandfather was Changyi, a District Magistrate; and his father was Du, an Assistant Prefect. His mother was née Ding. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Yi, Sui, Gai, a Supervising Secretary in the Office of Scrutiny for Revenue, Yi, and Xian; his younger brothers were Shan, Qian, Nie, Fa, Fang, and Zhi [?—the transcribed names 前、孽、蕟 are doubtful]. He married a woman née Wu. He ranked seventh in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 288th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰創業以武
守成以文昔人有
是說也然兵農一
心文武同方其用
果有異乎文武之
===
分始於何時兵民
之判起於何代嘗
質諸古矣書稱堯
曰乃武乃文於舜
稱文明禹稱文命

punctuated: 皇帝制曰：創業以武，守成以文，昔人有是說也。然兵農一心，文武同方，其用果有異乎？文武之分始於何時？兵民之判起於何代？嘗質諸古矣。《書》稱堯曰「乃武乃文」，於舜稱「文明」，禹稱「文命」，
translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “Founding a dynasty requires military prowess; preserving its achievements requires civil virtue.” Such was a saying of the ancients. Yet soldiers and farmers are of one mind, and civil and military affairs follow the same way. Do their functions truly differ? When did the distinction between civil and military affairs begin? In what age did the separation of soldiers from civilians arise? We have sought to examine these matters against antiquity. The Book of Documents describes Yao as “both martial and cultured”; of Shun it speaks of “cultured enlightenment,” and of Yu, “civilizing influence” …

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
而不及武於湯稱
聖武而不及文周
之謨烈各專其一
且三代迭尚而不
武周列四民而
不與焉何也漢
唐宋之英君令主
或創業而兼乎文
或守成而兼乎武
或有未備亦足以

translation_en: …yet makes no mention of martial qualities; of Tang it speaks of sagely martial prowess but makes no mention of civil qualities. The plans and achievements of the Zhou each concentrated on one of these. Moreover, the Three Dynasties successively esteemed different things but did not esteem martial affairs [?]; the Zhou enumerated four classes of people, yet soldiers were not included among them. Why was this? Among the outstanding sovereigns and worthy rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song, some founded dynasties while also possessing civil accomplishments; others preserved their inherited rule while also possessing martial prowess. Some may have lacked the full complement of these qualities, yet were still sufficiently able to…

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
善治論者又謂天
下安注意相又謂
天下雖安忘戰則
危是治兵之道果

punctuated: 善治。論者又謂：「天下安，注意相。」又謂：「天下雖安，忘戰則危。」是治兵之道果與治民者同邪，異邪？我太祖高皇帝以聖神文武統一天下，建官分籍，各有定制。列聖相承，率循是道。
translation_en: …govern well. Commentators also say, “When all under Heaven is at peace, give attention to the chief councillor,” and, “Though all under Heaven is at peace, forgetting warfare brings danger.” Is the way of governing the military, then, truly the same as that of governing the people, or is it different? Our founding emperor, Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, unified all under Heaven through his sagely and divine qualities and his civil and military prowess. He established offices and divided the population into registration categories, each with its prescribed institutions. The successive sage emperors inherited his rule and all followed this way.

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
臣楊愼
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下也有出治之全德有
保治之全功文武並用出治之全德也兵農相
資保治之全功也於並用而見其同方則天下
之政出於一而德爲全德如日月之在天凡所
以照臨者皆天之德也於相資而見其一致則
天下之治出於一而功爲全功如手足之在人
凡所以持行者皆人之功也由是聯屬天下以
成其道□□其道以適於治體統相承而無偏
□□本末具備而無罅隙可議之疵放
===
□□□□□準傳之萬世而無弊帝王爲治之
要舉不外於此哉臣自少讀帝王之書講帝王
之道竊有志於當世之事然學焉而不敢言言
焉而不得達今幸近
咫尺之威立方寸之地
制策所及者皆是道與是事也臣敢不罄一得之
愚以爲萬分之助乎伏覩
聖問首曰創業以武守成以文而又曰文武同方兵
農一致果有異乎臣惟三代而上同一道也戡
亂則曰武守成則曰文同一民也無事則爲農
alt_text:
臣楊慎
臣對臣聞帝王之御天下也有出治之全德有
保治之全功文武並用出治之全德也兵農相
資保治之全功也於並用而見其同方則天下
之政出於一而德為全德如日月之在天凡所
以照臨者皆天之德也於相資而見其一致則
天下之治出於一而功為全功如手足之在人
凡所以捍衛者皆人之功也由是聯屬天下以
成其身以其道以適於治體統相承而無偏
重本末具備而無罅隙可議之疵放
〇登科錄文　一
===
準傳之萬世而無弊帝王為治之
要事也此哉臣自少讀帝王之書講帝王
之道竊有志於當世之事然學焉而不敢言
焉而不得達今幸近
咫尺之威立方寸之地
制策所及者皆是道與是事也臣敢不罄一得之
愚以為萬分之助乎伏覩
聖問首曰創業以武守成以文而又曰文武同方兵
農一致果有異乎臣惟三代而上同一道也戡
亂則曰武守成則曰文同一民也無事則為農
punctuated:
臣楊愼。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御天下也，有出治之全德，有保治之全功。文武並用，出治之全德也；兵農相資，保治之全功也。於並用而見其同方，則天下之政出於一，而德爲全德，如日月之在天，凡所以照臨者，皆天之德也。於相資而見其一致，則天下之治出於一，而功爲全功，如手足之在人，凡所以持行者，皆人之功也。由是聯屬天下以成其道，□□其道以適於治，體統相承而無偏□□，本末具備而無罅隙可議之疵，放□□□□□準，傳之萬世而無弊。帝王爲治之要，舉不外於此哉！臣自少讀帝王之書，講帝王之道，竊有志於當世之事，然學焉而不敢言，言焉而不得達。今幸近咫尺之威，立方寸之地，制策所及者，皆是道與是事也。臣敢不罄一得之愚，以爲萬分之助乎？

伏覩聖問，首曰：「創業以武，守成以文。」而又曰：「文武同方，兵農一致，果有異乎？」臣惟三代而上，同一道也：戡亂則曰武，守成則曰文。同一民也：無事則爲農
translation_en:
Your servant, Yang Shen.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings govern All under Heaven, there is a completeness of virtue in establishing good government and a completeness of achievement in preserving it. Employing civil and military means together constitutes the completeness of virtue in establishing good government; having soldiers and farmers sustain one another constitutes the completeness of achievement in preserving it. When their common way is discerned in the joint employment of civil and military means, the policies of All under Heaven issue from a single source, and virtue becomes complete. This is like the sun and moon in heaven: all that they illuminate is illuminated through Heaven’s virtue. When their unity is discerned in the mutual support of soldiers and farmers, the good order of All under Heaven issues from a single source, and achievement becomes complete. This is like the hands and feet of a person: all their grasping and walking is accomplished through that person’s capacities. Thus All under Heaven is bound together to realize this Way; [two illegible characters] this Way to make it suited to governance. Its framework and order sustain one another without partiality [?]; root and branches are fully provided for, without gaps or flaws open to criticism. [The passage concerning its application as a standard is damaged and unclear.] It may be transmitted through ten thousand generations without harmful consequences. Surely the essentials of imperial and royal government lie entirely within this!

Since my youth, I have read the books of emperors and kings and studied their Way, privately aspiring to address the affairs of the present age. Yet, though I studied, I dared not speak; and when I spoke, my words could not reach the throne. Now I am fortunate to stand within a short distance of Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring presence, occupying this tiny space. Everything touched upon in the imperially issued policy question concerns precisely this Way and these affairs. How could I dare not exhaust whatever small insight my foolish mind possesses, in hopes of contributing even one ten-thousandth of assistance?

I have respectfully read Your Majesty’s question, which begins: “One establishes a dynasty by military means and preserves what has been achieved by civil means.” It further says: “Civil and military means share the same way; soldiers and farmers form a unity. Is there really any difference?” I submit that in the Three Dynasties and earlier, the Way was one and the same: when used to quell disorder, it was called military; when used to preserve established rule, it was called civil. The people were likewise one and the same: when there was no trouble, they were farmers…

〇登科錄文　二
punctuated:
有事則爲兵，初未始異也。在《易》，「明兩作，離」，文明之象也；「上九，王用出征，有嘉」，釋之者曰：「剛明及遠，威震而刑不濫。」斯不亦可見文武之同方乎？「地中有水，師」，師旅之象也，而釋之者曰：「伏至險於大順，藏不測於至靜。」盖寓兵於農之意，斯不亦可見兵農之一致乎？是故一張一弛，號爲善道；剛克柔克，協于皇極。周公冢宰，實兼東征；畢公爲公，亦以司馬。武夫堪腹心之寄，吉甫有文武之憲。太保治內，而未嘗無武；以采薇治外，□□□□，文武固未分也。自秦不師古，專以□□□□，語詩書者有刑，斬首級者進爵。民勇於戰，□□生好利之人，士賤以拘，廢干戈羽籥之習。至漢襲秦制，立丞相、將軍，而將相之職異；唐宋以來，置中書、元帥、樞密，而軍國之權偏。此文武之分出於三代之後也。

成周之制，以田賦出兵。一同之田，出戎馬四百匹、兵車百乘；一封之田，出戎馬四千匹、兵車千乘；畿方千里，提封萬井，出戎馬四萬匹、兵車萬乘。自五人爲伍，積而爲兩、爲卒；自五卒爲旅，積而爲師、爲軍。天子之六鄉六軍，諸侯之大國三軍、次國二軍、小國
translation_en:
…when there was trouble, they became soldiers: there had originally been no distinction. In the Book of Changes, “Brightness doubled constitutes Li” represents cultivated illumination. “Nine at the top: the king employs him to go forth on campaign; there is commendation.” A commentator explains: “Firmness and illumination reach afar; his might inspires awe, yet punishments are not excessive.” Does this not show that civil and military affairs follow the same way? “Water within the earth constitutes Shi” represents an army. A commentator explains: “The utmost danger lies concealed within the utmost compliance; the unfathomable is hidden within the utmost stillness.” This conveys the intention of lodging military service within agriculture. Does this not show the unity of soldiers and farmers? Thus, alternately drawing taut and relaxing was called the good way; mastery through firmness and mastery through gentleness accorded with the Sovereign’s Norm. The Duke of Zhou, as Minister of State, also undertook the eastern campaign; the Duke of Bi served as a duke and also as Minister of War. Warriors could be entrusted with the closest confidence, and Jifu provided a model of both civil and military accomplishment. The Grand Guardian governed internal affairs, yet was never without military capability; “Gathering Bracken” was employed in managing external affairs [?]. [Four illegible characters.] Civil and military affairs were certainly not yet divided. Qin ceased to take antiquity as its model and relied exclusively upon [four illegible characters]. Those who discussed the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents were punished, while those who cut off enemy heads advanced in noble rank. The people were bold in battle; [two illegible characters] produced people fond of profit [?]. Scholars were held in contempt for their rigidity, and the combined practice of arms and ritual dance with feathers and flutes fell into disuse. When Han inherited Qin’s institutions, it established posts of Chief Councilor and General, separating their duties. From Tang and Song onward, the establishment of the Secretariat, supreme commanders, and the Bureau of Military Affairs left military and state authority unevenly apportioned. Thus the division between civil and military affairs arose after the Three Dynasties.

Under the institutions of Zhou, military forces were supplied through levies on farmland. One tong of land furnished four hundred warhorses and one hundred war chariots; one feng of land furnished four thousand warhorses and one thousand war chariots. The royal domain, a thousand li square and encompassing ten thousand jing of land, furnished forty thousand warhorses and ten thousand war chariots. Five men formed a squad (wu); these were combined into platoons (liang) and companies (zu). Five companies formed a battalion (lü); these were combined into regiments (shi) and armies (jun). The Son of Heaven’s six townships furnished six armies. Among the domains of the feudal lords, a large state furnished three armies, a middle-ranking state two armies, and a small state…

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
一軍而降殺有等焉一方有事則命將出師迨
功成獻俘將歸于朝即守職之吏兵散于野即
緣畝之農兵農固未判也至管仲相齊欲速圖
覇業乃壞周兵於內政分四民以六鄉使國中
之民為兵鄙野之民為農兵不服耒耜之勤民
不識干戈之用以至司馬之木鐸秦招之銳士
成周之制壹掃蕩盡矣此兵農之判由於三代之
衰也載質之詩書所稱古之帝王未有不兼文
武之德而底平治之功者稱帝堯者曰乃武乃文
稱大禹者曰祗台德先不距朕行此所謂文也舜
===

命敷于四海之餘事也布昭聖武是于湯誠然聖謨
嘉言不為文武之全歟文謨武烈稱于君陳然
整旅伐桀下車訪道二者正未始偏廢也三代
迭尚曰忠曰質以文而不及武者蓋言忠質文
則武固在其中必以武言則是秦之所尚而非

一軍，而降殺有等焉。一方有事，則命將出師；迨功成獻俘，將歸于朝，即守職之吏；兵散于野，即緣畝之農。兵農固未判也。至管仲相齊，欲速圖覇業，乃壞周兵於內政，分四民以六鄉，使國中之民為兵，鄙野之民為農。兵不服耒耜之勤，民不識干戈之用，以至司馬之木鐸、秦招之銳士，成周之制壹掃蕩盡矣。此兵農之判，由於三代之衰也。
載質之詩書，所稱古之帝王，未有不兼文武之德而底平治之功者。稱帝堯者曰：「乃武乃文。」稱大禹者曰：「祗台德先，不距朕行。」此所謂文也。舜之格有苗，固所以武功著，而亦文命敷于四海之餘事也。「布昭聖武」，是于湯誠然；「聖謨嘉言」，不為文武之全歟？「文謨武烈」稱于君陳，然整旅伐桀、下車訪道，二者正未始偏廢也。三代迭尚，曰忠、曰質、以文，而不及武者，蓋言忠質文，則武固在其中；必以武言，則是秦之所尚，而非三代之治矣。周列四民，曰士農工商，而兵不與者，即臣前所陳寓兵於農之說；再以兵言，是為後世之制，而非成周之舊矣。漢唐宋之君，如光武之投戈講藝、太宗之身兼將相，庶幾創業而
translation_en:
…one army, with graded reductions in number. When trouble arose in a region, a commander was appointed and troops dispatched. Once victory had been achieved and captives presented, the commander returned to court and was once again an official attending to his duties; the soldiers dispersed into the countryside and were once again farmers working their fields. Soldiers and farmers had certainly not yet been separated. When Guan Zhong became chief minister of Qi, however, he sought to establish hegemony quickly. He therefore undermined Zhou military arrangements through domestic administration [?], dividing the four occupational groups among six districts, making the inhabitants of the capital soldiers and those of the outlying countryside farmers. Soldiers no longer endured the toil of plowing, while the people no longer understood the use of weapons. By the time of the Minister of War’s wooden-clapper bell and the elite troops of “Qin Zhao” [?], the institutions of Zhou had been swept away entirely. Thus the separation of soldiers from farmers originated in the decline of the Three Dynasties.
Turning also to the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents for verification, none of the ancient emperors and kings they praise failed to unite civil and martial virtue and thereby achieve peace and good government. In praise of Emperor Yao, it says: “Both martial and cultured.” In praise of Yu the Great, it says: “Reverently put my virtue first; do not oppose my conduct.” This is what is meant by civil virtue. Shun’s bringing the Youmiao into submission certainly manifested his martial achievements, yet it was also merely an incidental accomplishment alongside the spreading of his civil instruction throughout the Four Seas [?]. “He made his sagely martial might shine forth”: this was indeed true of Tang. Yet do “sagely counsels and excellent words” not constitute the completeness of both civil and martial virtue? “Civil counsels and martial achievements” are praised in the ‘Jun Chen’ chapter [?]. Yet marshaling the army to attack Jie and, on descending from his carriage, seeking instruction in the Way were two activities neither of which he ever neglected. The Three Dynasties successively esteemed loyalty, simplicity, and refinement. Martial virtue is not mentioned because it is already contained within loyalty, simplicity, and refinement. If martial prowess must be singled out, that is what Qin esteemed, rather than the government of the Three Dynasties. Zhou listed four occupational groups—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—without including soldiers. This is precisely the arrangement your servant explained earlier: embedding soldiers among farmers. To list soldiers separately would describe the institutions of later ages, rather than the ancient system of Zhou. … also combined this with civil accomplishments. As for those whose achievements were incomplete, one such example was Gaozu of Han: although he did not devote himself to the Odes and Documents, his designs were broad and far-reaching. His generosity, benevolence, and magnanimity implicitly accorded with the Way; moreover, could he not appreciate Lu Jia’s words on employing both civil and military means [?]? Emperor Xiaowu’s remorse and Emperor Xianzong of Tang’s pacification of Huaixi and Xishu came close to combining the preservation of an inherited realm with military achievement. As for those whose achievements were incomplete, consider Emperor Renzong’s reign: although Western Xia ran rampant, he brought about forty-two years of peace. His profound benevolence and abundant beneficence nurtured the foundations of the state; moreover, was he not able to employ the Confucian generals Han and Fan?
Lu Jia said, “When All under Heaven is at peace, direct your attention to the chief minister.” Thus, in peaceful times, one must cultivate civil virtue. The ruler takes the assessment and selection of chief ministers as his duty [?]. It is also said, “A general is needed only for great undertakings.” This concerns the management of troops. The Methods of the Minister of War (Sima fa) says, “Though All under Heaven is at peace, forgetting warfare inevitably brings danger.” Thus, while cultivating civil virtue, one must also maintain military preparedness. Hence the saying, “The gentleman puts weapons in order to guard against the unexpected.” As for the method of managing troops [?], training soldiers and practicing military skills are precisely the means of bringing warfare to an end. Managing troops and governing the people may differ, yet they are alike.
The Han military system was divided into the Southern and Northern Armies. The Southern Army was responsible for guarding the imperial palace, and the Northern Army for patrolling the capital. There were cavalrymen and selected infantry, as well as the chariot troops and cavalry of the northwest, the towered warships of the southeast, the crossbowmen of Linzi, and the swordsmen of Jingchu. All depended on the government for their provisions and were not enrolled among the common people. Discerning observers lamented how far this departed from antiquity and the inability to restore the ancient system: under the Han, governing the people and managing troops were separate matters.
The system established for the Tang militia (fubing) was particularly good. Soldiers were dispersed among the militia headquarters, while generals returned to court, thereby eliminating the source of turmoil. Men became soldiers at twenty and were discharged at sixty, so the people did not suffer the hardship of prolonged service. …the troops were not kept permanently assembled, with the troubles that entailed. Weapons and armor came from the people, as did grain for public use, so the state incurred no expense in maintaining the troops. Governing the people and governing the troops were one and the same; commentators therefore had good reason to commend this system as approaching that of antiquity. Under the Song system there were three [illegible] prefectural troops [?], the various offices, commanders-in-chief, military supervisors, and generals. Yet throughout the Song dynasty, the frontier [illegible]: this was because military authority was made too weak and soldiers were separated too completely from the people. Thus, “civil” and “military” are the names; soldiers and farmers are the substance. In the Three Dynasties and earlier, soldiers came from the farming population, so civil and military functions necessarily remained united. After the Three Dynasties, soldiers were separated from farmers, so civil and military functions necessarily became divided. The reasons for the relative weight accorded to civil and military functions in antiquity lay in the way the people and troops were governed [remainder illegible].
Our own [illegible] responded to Heaven and accorded with the people; all beings gave him their allegiance. He inaugurated what previous dynasties had never possessed [illegible] settlement [?]. His achievements established rites and music to augment the established statutes [?]; his grand designs arose in the aftermath of the transformation under the barbarian Yuan [?], and he fostered civil teaching in a land where armed struggle had restored rightful order. How flourishing, then, was his civil virtue! When offices were established at that time, court ranks comprised civil and military ranks; the official establishment comprised civil and military posts; and the ministries included bureaus for civil and military appointments. When registers were established, permanent landed property comprised military agricultural colonies and civilian fields; household registration comprised military and civilian registers; and administrative offices comprised prefectures and counties, guards and battalions. With the sovereign exercising sole decision through Heaven-like firmness, there was no loss of commanding authority to subordinates. With jurisdictions interlocking like a dog's teeth and checking one another, there was no danger of a tail grown too large to wag. When affairs arose, civil and military officials jointly participated in confidential deliberations; when affairs were quiet, each discharged his entrusted responsibility for troops or people. In the capital, the Minister of War supervised the military camps; outside the capital, there were censorial officials…

…to exercise overall command of frontier affairs. The provincial surveillance commissions oversee military preparedness, while county officials specialize in patrolling and apprehending offenders. Their designations seem separate, yet in practice they are interconnected; their duties seem distinct, yet their responsibilities sustain one another. These methods of preserving good government accord with those of the Three Dynasties. Taizong honored and promoted the classics and histories while also pacifying the disturbances in the northern deserts. Xuanzong esteemed Confucian officials while going forth to suppress the rebellion of the Prince of Han. Successive sage emperors continued these efforts with ever greater diligence and dedication. For a hundred and fifty years, all have achieved good government through civil culture, while court strategy has overlooked nothing and divine martial power has prevailed without killing. [Three illegible characters] in rites and music, without abandoning [two illegible characters] these people [?]; indeed, there are those who follow this way without understanding it.
I reverently reflect that Your Majesty, possessing this abundant inheritance, considers plans for daily renewal. Your extensive experience brings clear understanding of principle; your profound self-cultivation brings steadfast resolve. You let your robes hang and fold your hands, and all under Heaven turn toward your influence; you change your expression, and all within the seas tremble in awe. You extinguish dangers on the frontier just as they flare up and dissolve troubles within the palace walls before they take shape. Men of virtue cleanse their hearts to receive your excellent virtue, while the common people crane their necks in expectation of great peace. Yet Your Majesty remains humble, observing that, when peace has endured for long, negligence and complacency follow. Having reverently read this far, your servant recognizes that Your Majesty’s full virtue in establishing good government and your complete achievement in preserving it can be realized through this single thought.

Your servant humbly believes that Your Majesty’s desire for good government is most earnest, yet those charged with carrying it out may not have fully fulfilled it. Schools are the foremost influence on customs. Cheng Yi said that governing the realm rests upon correcting customs and obtaining worthy talent. If all those placed in charge of schools were suitable men, and their methods of instruction were entirely like those of Yang Cheng at the Directorate of Education and Hu Yuan at the school in Huzhou, they would unify moral teaching to clarify ritual propriety and righteousness, and concentrate on classical learning to establish sound habits. Learning would then neither be neglected through amusement nor ruined through unthinking conformity. An atmosphere of sincerity and generosity could prevail [?], and there would be no need to worry about scholars neglecting their proper calling. The people are the foundation upon which the state depends. Shao Yong said that every measure of leniency brings the people a corresponding measure of benefit. What is valued … lies in … [?]; nothing is more immediately important than prefects and county magistrates. If all those appointed prefects and county magistrates were suitable men, entirely like Huang Ba in Yingchuan and Zhang Yong in Yizhou, they would observe the provisions of imperial edicts and proclaim Your Majesty’s benevolent intentions. They would not put extracting revenue ahead of protecting the people, nor place nurturing them after pressing for taxes. Prosperity among the people could then be expected, and there would be no need to worry about people reporting hunger.
That displaced people eventually gather together as bandits likewise results from a lack of proper methods of instruction and of sustained provision for their livelihood. In terms of human feelings, bandits too are simply people. Everyone cherishes their strength and their body; everyone cherishes their parents, wife, and children; everyone cherishes their fields, home, and possessions. Even when misfortune brings death, they are unwilling to relinquish what they cherish; how much less would they abandon it to enter a place of certain death? Yet today, those who take up arms beside the pools and proclaim themselves leaders in the greenwoods are everywhere. Taxes are exacted excessively, with autumn assessments drawn upon in spring; the abuses of transporting provisions leave nine households out of ten empty. Agriculture must receive serious attention. Recently, Your Majesty released two hundred thousand taels of silver from the privy treasury to supplement military supplies in western Shu. Your love for the people may indeed be called profound. Military administration especially demands urgent attention. Recently, [three illegible characters] three thousand cavalrymen of the military camps were employed to pacify the disaffected in Shandong. Your efforts to ward off trouble may be called [illegible]. Your foolish servant believes that the able-bodied men of the locality should themselves be employable. Formerly, when the Han fought the Xiongnu, they employed sons of respectable families from the Six Commanderies. These men knew the difficult and easy terrain thoroughly and fought hard to defend their native places; compared with troops mobilized from elsewhere, one could match a hundred. translation_en:
…if the proper way is followed, even the greedy and the deceitful can be employed—how much more those who harbor virtue [?] and aspire to achievement and renown! The system of selection and appointment is impartial; yet might there not be pedantic scholars entrusted with affairs, while those [?] capable of governing are relegated to idle posts? The rules for demotion and promotion are fitting; yet might there not be men who consume stipends merely to fill positions, and cause to lament worthy men left obscure and talent overlooked? The commands governing rewards and punishments are clear; yet might there not be incompetents who receive rewards, and men who “wear a basin over their heads” [?] yet escape punishment?

If every office truly obtained the right man, every talent were fully employed, everyone possessed the impartiality that forgets private interests, and every undertaking expressed sincere devotion to the country, we would gather mulberry roots to secure the nest before the sky grew overcast, and move the piled firewood before a fire broke out. When one prefecture faced an alarm, neighboring prefectures would keenly feel the anxiety of danger close at hand; when an alarm arose, beforehand [?] the regret of trying to bite one’s own navel—regret that comes too late. When the enemy arrived, we would not fear; when he departed, we would not treat him with contempt. We would not depend on others [?] troops, nor prolong operations and exhaust our resources. Within [?], fully beyond the scope of regulations and instruction [?]; the abuses of civil officials’ complacency and military officials’ negligence [?] would certainly be prohibited.

The diffusion of civil virtue would be like clouds moving and rain falling; the establishment of military achievement would be like fierce thunder and swift wind. In its far-reaching effects, this could restore the good government of the ancient emperors and kings; above, it could bring glory to the plans and achievements of your imperial ancestors. The dynasty’s allotted span, lasting hundreds of millions of years, could endure alongside Heaven and Earth without end. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would further exalt this virtue and further preserve these achievements, maintain a heart free from negligence and dissipation, and pursue a way capable of enduring and becoming great. If, amid the myriad affairs of government, you would spare this a little attention, then everything about which you have questioned your servant could, in due sequence, be…

臣對：臣聞天下無一定之勢，故治天下不可□一偏之用。文武者，治天下之用也。文以致太平，武以定禍亂，二者之為用，其功一也。然機之來也無常，而勢之變也靡定，意外之虞恒在於太平之世。恃其太平也，溺於文而無武事之備，則患將起而無所資，固為一偏之用。知武可以除患矣，不求其致患之由起於文教之敝，則用武□□□□乎為用之全，而可以成治哉？故論治□□□□者，不知機者也；守文而不兼乎武□□□□□□者，不善治者也。治忽有相倚之機，□□□□兼資之用，是固唐虞三代之所以成治，漢唐宋之所以小康，我太祖高皇帝之所以並駕乎唐虞三代而陋漢唐宋於下風者也。

translation_en:
Your servant, Yu Ben.

Your servant replies: I have heard that circumstances in the realm are never fixed; thus, in governing the realm, one must not [illegible] rely on only one means. Civil and military measures are the means of governing the realm. Civil measures bring about great peace; military measures quell calamity and disorder. In their application, the two serve the same end. Yet opportunities arise unpredictably, and changing circumstances have no fixed course. The danger of unforeseen events is ever present in an age of great peace. If one relies on that peace, becomes engrossed in civil affairs, and makes no military preparations, then trouble will arise with no resources available to meet it. This is certainly a one-sided application of these means. If one knows that military measures can eliminate trouble but does not investigate how that trouble arose from the deterioration of civil instruction, then can the use of military measures [four characters illegible] constitute a complete application of these means and achieve good government? Thus, those who discuss government [four characters illegible] do not understand the opportunities presented by circumstances; those who adhere to civil measures without also employing military ones [six characters illegible] are not skilled at governing. Good government and disorder contain the potential to give rise to one another; [four characters illegible] the use of both means in mutual support. This was indeed how the rulers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties achieved good government, and how the Han, Tang, and Song achieved a lesser degree of tranquility. It was also how our Emperor Taizu Gao kept pace with Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties, leaving the Han, Tang, and Song inferior and far behind.

I reverently reflect that Your Majesty the Emperor, in the prime of life, has presided over an era of flourishing accomplishment for six years now. You have eliminated the wicked and removed [𧧼: unclear], undertaking great endeavors with awe-inspiring vigor, omitting nothing in either civil affairs or military preparedness. If you fully exerted your gifts of intelligence and divine martial prowess, would these not suffice to achieve the government of grand harmony attained by the ancient emperors and kings? Yet you do not consider yourself fully accomplished. In your edict posing policy questions to the candidates, you remain earnestly concerned, asking about the combined use of civil and military measures; and, at a time of peace [天平: uncertain reading] …

…at the height of prosperity, you feel profound concern about unforeseen dangers and seek ways to avert them. Your servant can thus glimpse Your Majesty’s intentions: so earnest is your concern that you will surely act with resolve. Indeed, you truly are a ruler destined for great accomplishments! While living in the countryside, I have privately reflected on the affairs of the realm and eagerly wished to speak, but have had no opportunity. Now I have encountered Your Majesty as you prepare to undertake great things; moreover, you have summoned us and invited us to speak. If I were still to remain silent at this moment, would I not betray my own conscience? I beg to lay before Your Majesty everything I have wished throughout my life to say. Military preparations must therefore also be undertaken when civil governance flourishes. I have examined how the emperors and kings of antiquity governed: while esteeming civil governance to bring about the fullness of great peace, they invariably also employed military measures to guard against unforeseen dangers. …formed a company (zu); five companies formed a battalion (lü), five battalions an army (jun), and five armies a host (shi). [?] Thus the men of these companies, battalions, armies, and hosts were precisely the people of the neighborhood and township groupings—bi, lü, zu, dang, zhou, and xiang. How could generals who soared like hawks and struck fiercely like tigers be distinct from the ministers who exchanged assent and counsel, bowed, and yielded courteously? Soldiers and farmers were united [?]; hence, wherever farmers gathered, soldiers were already present. Civil and military affairs followed the same course; hence, as civil culture spread, military strength also flourished. Their operation was fundamentally undivided, and government was therefore balanced. Thus “Chariot Attack” (Che gong) and “Auspicious Day” (Ji ri) helped revive the neglected institutions of the great royal order [?], while the dispatch of troops in “The Sixth Month” (Liu yue) achieved victory over the Xianyun.
Alas! Qi pursued quick results and material advantage. It consequently established its system of internal administration, and soldiers and farmers began to stand apart. Yet military administration was said to be embedded within that system: although the ancient conception had been damaged, the relationship between soldiers and farmers had not yet entirely [?]. Seven commandants were added, and towered warships were deployed outside, establishing arrangements for long-term service and garrison stations [?]; the soldiers became separated from the farmers. Qin prized military achievement, and consequently military achievement [?] showed signs of a contrast involving military affairs [?]. Yet, with a single chief minister exercising overall command, the authority over [?] military affairs had not yet been wholly divided. Under the Song, the people came under the chief ministers, while military matters were entrusted to the Bureau of Military Affairs. This established the rule that the two administrations should exercise separate responsibilities, and military affairs then became separated from civil affairs. The separation of soldiers from farmers brought the expense of maintaining troops: farmers suffered hardship, yet the military still failed to flourish. The separation of military from civil affairs encouraged arguments disparaging military pursuits: military strength declined, while civil administration likewise achieved nothing.
From this we may say that uniting soldiers and farmers and employing both civil and military means was the sound method of antiquity; separating soldiers from farmers and placing unequal emphasis on civil and military means was the defective government of later ages. Emperor Taizong of the Tang told his ministers: “Found a dynasty through military means; preserve its achievements through civil means.” His essential intention was to promote government through civil instruction after military success had been secured; he therefore spoke only of what deserved the greater emphasis. 聖制所及唐虞三代質之。益之称堯曰：「乃武乃文。」是固文武之兼用矣。然舜稱文明，禹稱文命，文稱顯謨，而不及武者，豈謂三聖偏主於文而不兼用乎武哉？顧以三聖之所以守成者重於文，文教舉而武自不廢也。不然，則有苗分北、防風受戮、戡黎而伐崇者，果何為哉？於湯稱聖武，於武稱承烈，而不及文者，又豈謂二聖偏主於武而不兼用乎文哉？顧以二聖之所以定亂者重於武，□□而文自大敷也。不然，則纘禹舊服，政□□□何為哉？三代異忠質文之尚，不言□□□□於內，則其忠質文之所尚已有武□□□農工賈之名，兵不與焉。然兵寓於農，則其農之所畜即為兵也。是則唐虞三代之所以用其文武，其有偏舉而能成治者哉？
臣請更以聖制所及漢唐宋之英君令主質之。漢之光武、唐之太宗、宋之藝祖，以武而創業者也。然投戈講藝，息馬論道，增館舍而大召名儒，視大學而親題聖贊，其不兼乎文哉？此所以粗有太平之象焉。漢之文帝、唐之憲宗、宋之太宗，以文而守成者
translation_en:
…the eras of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties mentioned in Your Majesty’s decree, to test this proposition. Yi praised Yao, saying, “Both martial and civil.” This certainly means employing both civil and military means. Yet Shun was praised for his “civil refinement and enlightenment,” Yu for his “civilizing commands,” and King Wen for his “illustrious counsels,” without mention of military qualities. Does this mean that these three sages favored civil means alone and did not also employ military means? It is simply that, in preserving an established order, these three sages placed greater weight on civil means. When civil instruction flourished, military affairs were naturally not neglected. Otherwise, what purpose was served by dispersing the Youmiao, executing Fangfeng, subduing Li, and attacking Chong?
Tang was praised for his “sagely martial prowess,” and King Wu for “carrying forward glorious achievements,” without mention of civil qualities. Does this, in turn, mean that these two sages favored military means alone and did not also employ civil means? It is simply that, in suppressing disorder, these two sages placed greater weight on military means. [Two illegible characters] and civil influence naturally spread far and wide. Otherwise, what purpose was served by continuing Yu’s former undertakings and by governing [three illegible characters; sense uncertain] [?]? The Three Dynasties differed in their esteem for loyalty, simplicity, and refinement. The passage concerning what was “not spoken of” and what was “within” is damaged [?]; what they esteemed in loyalty, simplicity, and refinement already included military qualities [text damaged] [?]. Among the designations of farmers, artisans, and merchants, soldiers were not included. Yet soldiers were incorporated among the farmers, so those maintained among the farmers were themselves soldiers. Thus, in their employment of civil and military means, could Tang, Yu, or the Three Dynasties have achieved good government by emphasizing only one?
Your servant asks further to test this proposition against the outstanding rulers and excellent sovereigns of the Han, Tang, and Song mentioned in Your Majesty’s decree. Guangwu of the Han, Taizong of the Tang, and Yizu of the Song founded their dynasties through military means. Yet they laid aside their spears to discuss the arts of learning, rested their horses to discourse on the Way, enlarged scholarly establishments and summoned renowned Confucian scholars in great numbers, and visited the Imperial University and personally inscribed imperial encomia. Did they not also employ civil means? This is why their reigns displayed at least some semblance of great peace. Emperor Wen of the Han, Xianzong of the Tang, and Taizong of the Song were rulers who preserved an established order through civil means…

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
也然躬御戎馬削平藩鎮討契丹而中夏增氣
志恢復而名分稍正其不兼乎武哉此所以亦
無危亂之虞焉不然則牽制文義漢室以衰窮
黷兵革唐室大亂文武不備而求欲善治寧有
是哉陸賈之告陳平曰天下安注意相是固以
太平右文為說然司馬法曰天下雖安忘戰必
危則又以太平不可無武為言意各有指言固
並行而不相悖也治兵之道豈有異於治民者
□□患以除患既除而民即安矣是則
□□□□無非文武之道故能成太和之治
□□□□□言今主雖於分判兵農之後不失
□□□□□武之意故亦收小康之功也恭惟我
太祖高皇帝以聖神文武之德成華夷一統之功文
武建官而府衛無偏舉之弊兵農分籍而彼此
定稽察之公執干戈以任殺伐是固兵矣而參
機務者必以憲臣主之制總統者必以兵部主
之文武雖判其有偏廢邪出賦稅以給公上是
固農矣而分衛所者亦有屯田之規割田畝者
又有寄莊之令兵農雖分其復有偏用邪
聖聖相承率循是道百五十年治定功成實由於此

○登科錄文　十五
===
今主雖於分判兵農之後不失
□□之意故亦收小康之功也恭惟我
皇帝以聖神文武之德成華夷一統之功文

之文武雖判其有偏廢耶出賦稅以給公上是
固農矣而分衛所者亦有屯田之規制□畝者
又有寄莊之令兵農雖分其復有偏用耶
聖聖相承率循是道百五十年治定功成實□於此
punctuated:
也。然躬御戎馬，削平藩鎮，討契丹而中夏增氣，志恢復而名分稍正，其不兼乎武哉？此所以亦無危亂之虞焉。不然，則牽制文義，漢室以衰；窮黷兵革，唐室大亂。文武不備而求欲善治，寧有是哉？陸賈之告陳平曰：「天下安，注意相。」是固以太平右文為說。然《司馬法》曰：「天下雖安，忘戰必危。」則又以太平不可無武為言。意各有指，言固並行而不相悖也。治兵之道，豈有異於治民者？□□患以除患，既除而民即安矣。是則□□□□無非文武之道，故能成太和之治。□□□□□言今主，雖於分判兵農之後，不失□□□□□武之意，故亦收小康之功也。
恭惟我太祖高皇帝，以聖神文武之德，成華夷一統之功。文武建官，而府衛無偏舉之弊；兵農分籍，而彼此定稽察之公。執干戈以任殺伐，是固兵矣，而參機務者必以憲臣主之，制總統者必以兵部主之。文武雖判，其有偏廢邪？出賦稅以給公上，是固農矣，而分衛所者亦有屯田之規，割田畝者又有寄莊之令。兵農雖分，其復有偏用邪？聖聖相承，率循是道，百五十年，治定功成，實由於此。
translation_en:
…Yet they personally took command of their warhorses and troops, subdued the regional military commands, attacked the Khitan and thereby raised the spirit of the Central Lands, and aspired to restoration, thereby somewhat rectifying the proper order of status and authority. Did they not also employ military means? This is why they, too, were free from the prospect of peril and disorder. Otherwise, constrained by civil and literary principles, the Han dynasty declined; through unrestrained warfare, the Tang dynasty fell into great disorder. Could good government possibly be achieved without providing for both civil and military affairs? Lu Jia told Chen Ping: “When All under Heaven is at peace, attend to the chief minister.” This certainly advocates giving precedence to civil affairs in times of peace. Yet the Methods of the Minister of War (Sima fa) says: “Though All under Heaven is at peace, forgetting warfare inevitably brings danger.” This, in turn, says that military preparedness cannot be dispensed with in times of peace. Each statement has its particular point; the two can indeed be followed together without contradiction. How could the way of governing troops differ from that of governing the people? [Illegible] trouble in order to eliminate trouble [?]; once it is eliminated, the people are secure. Thus [illegible] all belonged to the way of civil and military governance, and so could bring about government in perfect harmony. [Illegible passage concerning rulers; wording uncertain][?] Even after soldiers and farmers had been separated, they did not lose the intent of [illegible] military affairs [?], and thus also achieved a measure of well-being.
I reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, through his sagely and divine virtue in civil and military affairs, accomplished the unification of the Chinese and the non-Chinese peoples. He established civil and military offices, so that the military commissions and guards suffered no imbalance from favoring one side; he placed soldiers and farmers on separate registers, establishing impartial scrutiny of both. Those who wield weapons and undertake killing and punitive expeditions are certainly soldiers. Yet censorial officials must preside over those who participate in confidential military deliberations, and the Ministry of War must direct the arrangements for overall command. Although civil and military affairs are distinct, is either neglected? Those who furnish taxes to supply the government are certainly farmers. Yet there are also regulations for military agricultural colonies among those assigned to guards and battalions, and orders concerning outlying landed holdings (jizhuang) for those allotted fields [?]. Although soldiers and farmers are distinct, is one again employed to the exclusion of the other? Sage sovereign has succeeded sage sovereign, all following this way. That government has been firmly established and great achievements accomplished over these hundred and fifty years is truly due to this.

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
雖然亦由其先有文以為之本耳方今承平既
久釁孽或萌是以潢池盜賊有弄兵之虞將欲
治之固不可不求之武事之備然求其所由起
又豈徒武事不振之弊哉備武事於文教大敷
之際則先有文教以為之本故武事備而患無
由興使徒用武事於盜賊既起之後則已無文
教以懷其心武將不戢而患愈大故易曰豶豕
之牙吉祭公謀父亦曰先王耀德不觀兵蓋必
有文以定其本夫然後可以振武事以張
===
□□□法具存而士或失業蠲貸之詔屢
而□多令饑流徙之餘化為盜賊夫以盜賊
起於流徙則其所以致之之由固不徒在於武
事之弛矣且盜賊以梟獍之性自速危亡之禍
豈其情獨惡生全而樂危亡哉饑寒切身而禮
義無以養其心治之者又以峻法虐政奪其資
