punctuated: 雖然，亦由其先有文以為之本耳。方今承平既久，釁孽或萌，是以潢池盜賊有弄兵之虞。將欲治之，固不可不求之武事之備；然求其所由起，又豈徒武事不振之弊哉？備武事於文教大敷之際，則先有文教以為之本，故武事備而患無由興。使徒用武事於盜賊既起之後，則已無文教以懷其心，武將不戢而患愈大。故《易》曰：「豶豕之牙，吉。」祭公謀父亦曰：「先王耀德不觀兵。」蓋必有文以定其本，夫然後可以振武事以張□□□。法具存，而士或失業；蠲貸之詔屢，而□多令饑。流徙之餘，化為盜賊。夫以盜賊起於流徙，則其所以致之之由，固不徒在於武事之弛矣。且盜賊以梟獍之性，自速危亡之禍，豈其情獨惡生全而樂危亡哉？饑寒切身，而禮義無以養其心；治之者又以峻法虐政奪其資，而迫之使無所容。彼思均□死耳，死於盜賊，或可以緩旦夕之命，是以遂迫於禍而發。嗚呼！欲弭盜賊之患，其可以徒咎夫武事之弛，而不反其本哉？必也下
translation_en:
Nevertheless, this too was because civil cultivation had first provided the foundation. Now that peace has long prevailed, seeds of disorder may sprout, and there is thus a danger that petty bandits will take up arms. To bring them under control, military preparedness must certainly be sought. Yet, if we investigate why they arise, can the cause lie solely in the failure to maintain military strength? When military preparations are made while civil instruction flourishes, that instruction already provides the foundation. Military affairs are therefore in readiness, and trouble has no means of arising. If military force alone is employed after bandits have already risen, there is no longer civil instruction to win over their hearts. Warfare will then remain unchecked, and the trouble will grow still greater. Thus the Book of Changes says: “The tusks of a castrated boar: auspicious.” Zhai Gong Moufu also said: “The former kings displayed their virtue, not their military force.” Civil cultivation must first establish the foundation; only then can military affairs be strengthened to extend … [?].

The established measures all remain in place, yet some scholars have lost their livelihoods. Edicts granting remissions and relief have repeatedly been issued, yet many … suffer hunger [?]. After wandering in displacement, people turn into bandits. Since banditry arises from displacement, the reasons that bring it about assuredly do not lie solely in lax military preparedness. Moreover, although bandits, with the nature of owls and jing beasts—creatures proverbial for devouring their parents—bring the calamity of destruction upon themselves, can it be that they alone hate survival and delight in ruin? Hunger and cold press upon their bodies, while ritual propriety and righteousness have no means of nourishing their hearts. Those who govern them further use harsh laws and oppressive policies to take away their resources, pressing them until they have nowhere to find refuge. They think that either way they must die [?]; if they die as bandits, they may at least prolong lives otherwise likely to end at any moment. Thus, driven into calamity, they rise in revolt. Alas! If we wish to quell the scourge of banditry, can we merely blame lax military preparedness without returning to the root of the matter? It is essential to issue …

選良吏以任守令使困者有復蘇之望建良將
以任兵權使叛者有反正之依如此則盜賊動

練兵厲武大振九伐之威以繼之則威因惠立

===

□□□□也不然則官雖間得其人彼知所
以懐其心者甚少而我之所以為之病者甚多

punctuated:
寬恩之詔，明逆順之歸，事循先王之舊典，絕無後世之陋規。興學校以養其亷恥，深德澤以濟其饑寒，苛刑不以迫之也，橫歛不以奪之也。之然後，選良吏以任守令，使困者有復蘇之望；建良將以任兵權，使叛者有反正之依。如此，則盜賊動心，而首惡渠魁自將無所藉口以誘其眾。由是練兵厲武，大振九伐之威以繼之，則威因惠立，武以文奮。彼山澤嘯聚者，即渙然離散，而無以□□除，軍食自不必運而無不給矣。於□□教之治，兼資武事之脩，庶天下兵□□□□而相衞相養於無事之天。此誠久□□□□也。不然，則官雖間得其人，彼知所以懐其心者甚少，而我之所以為之病者甚多，患且日深，恐有猝未能弭者。是惡可不深探其本，究敷文教以為用武之資，而徒諉曰武事之不脩哉？以是而言，古之不偏用夫文者，盖兼武事於敷文之後也；臣之願不偏用夫武者，謂有所懲於文敝之餘也。

然臣猶有獻焉。天下之治，雖在於尚文而振武，而其本尤在於陛下之一心。心一正，則大本立而萬事定，農由是而
translation_en:
…an edict of generous clemency, making clear where rebellion and obedience respectively lead, conducting affairs according to the established statutes of the former kings, and wholly eliminating the defective practices of later ages. Establish schools to nurture their sense of integrity and shame, and deepen your beneficence to relieve their hunger and cold. Do not drive them into desperation with harsh punishments or strip them of their resources through arbitrary exactions. Then [?] select worthy officials to serve as prefects and magistrates, so that those in distress may hope to recover; appoint worthy generals to exercise military authority, so that rebels may have someone to rely upon in returning to allegiance. In this way, the bandits will be moved, and their chief malefactors and ringleaders will naturally have no pretext with which to entice their followers. Follow this by training troops and sharpening military preparedness, greatly displaying the might of the nine forms of punitive expedition. Authority will then be established through kindness, and military strength invigorated through civil governance. Those who gather in bands in the mountains and marshes will promptly disperse, with no means to … [?]. Supplies for the army will naturally be sufficient without even needing to be transported. Through governance by … instruction [?], drawing also upon cultivated military preparedness, it may be hoped that the troops throughout the realm … [?] will protect and sustain one another in a world at peace. This would indeed be lasting … [?]. Otherwise, even if offices occasionally obtain suitable men, those people know very little that would win their hearts [?], while we do much that causes them suffering. The trouble will deepen daily, and I fear that something may arise suddenly that cannot be quelled. How, then, can we fail to probe deeply into its roots and fully extend civil instruction as the foundation for employing military force, merely laying the blame on neglected military preparedness? Viewed in this light, when the ancients did not rely exclusively on civil measures, it was because they also attended to military affairs after extending civil instruction. When your servant wishes not to rely exclusively on military measures, I mean that we must take warning from the aftermath of the deterioration of civil governance.

Yet your servant still has something to offer. Although the ordering of the realm depends upon esteeming civil governance and invigorating military strength, its foundation lies above all in the single heart of Your Majesty. Once the heart is rectified, the great foundation is established and all affairs are settled. Farmers will thereby …

translation_en: …will have sustenance; through this, soldiers can be trained, civil virtue cultivated, and military achievement invigorated. Through this, the glorious deeds of your imperial ancestors will gain further lustre, and the good government of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties can be restored. The teaching of rectifying the mind has indeed been the essential way by which emperors and kings have governed the realm since antiquity. Such is the extent of your servant’s humble insight, acquired through long familiarity with exposition and recitation. I now venture to offer it to Your Sagacious Majesty. If Your Majesty would graciously give it a little consideration, the realm would be most fortunate, and the people most fortunate. In presuming to address Your Heavenly Majesty, your servant trembles with boundless fear. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

臣鄒守益
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也有安定天下之大功
有化成天下之大德安定之功在乎武化成之
德在乎文敷文教而擇人以治民則民安而文
德洽修武備而擇人以治兵則兵強而武功立
惟文武並用故功德兼隆此唐虞三代與我
朝之所以久安長治而非漢唐宋以下之所能逮
者也恭惟
皇帝陛下
撫盈成之運懷盈成之憂科貢慎選蠲貸屢下
揆育文德之繇振武功亦𧹞是其
===
進臣等於
廷首舉創業守成之文武異同為言次及於二
帝三王與漢唐宋諸君之得失末復及於
聖祖之定制與今日守成玩愒之弊而欲求所以保
長久之業是即堯舜禹湯文武之用心也即我
祖宗列聖之用心也臣敢不披瀝肝膽以對揚休命
於萬一臣聞帝王治天下之道大要有二曰文
與武而已仁以育天下故凡獎崇儒彥懷保黔
黎所以經緯天地而為化成之德者文之屬也

臣鄒守□
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也有所安定天下之大功
有化成天下之大德安定之功在乎武化成之
德在乎文敷文教而擇人以治民則民安而文
德合修武備而擇人以治兵則兵強而武功立
惟文武並用故功德無隆此唐虞三代與我
朝之所以久安長治而非漢唐宋以下之所能逮
也恭惟

□育文德訓敷武功亦根是其
敢進臣學術於
===
請明首舉創業之成之文武異同而言次及於二
帝三王與漢唐宋諸君之得失矣復及於
聖祖之定制與今日之玩偈之弊而欲知所以保
長久之業是即究文武之偏輔文武之用心也即我
祖宗列聖之用心也臣敢不披瀝肝膽以對揚休命
於萬一臣聞帝王治天下之道大要有二曰文
與武而已仁以育天下故凡奬崇儒教保黎
黎于以經緯天地而爲化成之德皆文之屬也
punctuated:
臣鄒守益。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御世也，有安定天下之大功，有化成天下之大德。安定之功在乎武，化成之德在乎文。敷文教而擇人以治民，則民安而文德洽；修武備而擇人以治兵，則兵強而武功立。惟文武並用，故功德兼隆。此唐虞三代與我朝之所以久安長治，而非漢唐宋以下之所能逮者也。恭惟皇帝陛下，撫盈成之運，懷盈成之憂，科貢慎選，蠲貸屢下。揆育文德之繇，振武功亦𧹞是。其進臣等於廷，首舉創業守成之文武異同為言，次及於二帝三王與漢唐宋諸君之得失，末復及於聖祖之定制與今日守成玩愒之弊，而欲求所以保長久之業。是即堯舜禹湯文武之用心也，即我祖宗列聖之用心也。臣敢不披瀝肝膽，以對揚休命於萬一？

臣聞帝王治天下之道，大要有二，曰文與武而已。仁以育天下，故凡獎崇儒彥、懷保黔黎，所以經緯天地而為化成之德者，文之屬也。
translation_en:
Your servant, Zou Shouyi.

Your servant replies: I have heard that emperors and kings, in governing the world, achieve great deeds that bring peace and stability to all under Heaven, and exercise great virtue that transforms and perfects all under Heaven. The achievement of peace and stability rests on military measures; the virtue that transforms and perfects rests on civil measures. When they spread civil instruction and choose men to govern the people, the people are at peace and civil virtue permeates the realm. When they attend to military preparations and choose men to command the troops, the troops are strong and military achievements are established. Only by employing civil and military measures together can achievement and virtue both flourish. This is why the reigns of Tang Yao and Yu Shun, the Three Dynasties, and our own dynasty have enjoyed enduring peace and lasting good government, beyond what the Han, Tang, Song, and subsequent dynasties could attain.

I respectfully consider that Your Majesty the Emperor presides over an age of abundance and established achievement, yet cherishes concern about preserving that abundance and achievement. You exercise care in selecting men through the examinations and tribute recommendations, and have repeatedly issued orders for tax remissions and relief loans. You consider the means of cultivating civil virtue and likewise seek to advance military achievement [?]. In summoning us, your servants, to court, you first raised the similarities and differences in civil and military measures between founding a dynasty and preserving its accomplishments. You next addressed the successes and failures of the Two Emperors, the Three Kings, and the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song. Finally, you turned to the established institutions of the sagely founding ancestor and the present abuses of complacency and idle delay in preserving the dynasty’s accomplishments, seeking the means to secure its enduring rule. This is precisely the concern of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu; it is precisely the concern of all the sage emperors among our dynastic ancestors. How could I, your servant, dare not lay bare my innermost thoughts, in the hope of responding to and extolling even a ten-thousandth part of your gracious command?

I have heard that the way emperors and kings govern all under Heaven has, in essence, only two aspects: the civil and the military. Through benevolence they nurture all under Heaven. Thus, rewarding and honoring outstanding Confucian scholars, cherishing and protecting the common people—all the means by which they order Heaven and Earth and exercise the virtue that transforms and perfects—belong to the civil sphere.

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
義以正天下故凡選擇將帥振勵卒伍干以消
折奸宄而為安定之功皆武之屬也有武而無
文以濟之則過於義而傷於剛無以存仁厚之
治體有文而無武以濟之則過於仁而流於柔
無以立精明之治功故是二者猶天之二氣不
可相勝猶車之二輪不可缺一陸賈所謂長久
之術其在是也然所謂創業以武守成以文是
蓋各就其重者言之耳如使創業者而無事乎
文則紀綱民物五教者非邪如使守成者
□□克詰戎兵張皇六師者非邪慨
===
□□□□□□□□武分井田壞而兵農判文事簿
□□□玩各職其職矣兵執干戈民執耒
耜□乃事其事矣德兵農一致文武同方古之
法豈不可復於今邪蓋嘗質諸古矣欽明文思
濬哲文明文命之敷人紀之肇脩五教之克
寬堯舜禹湯文武之文德也四凶之誅三苗之
征防風之戮升陘之師牧野之戰堯舜禹湯文
武之武功也彼稱堯之德曰乃武乃文舉其
全而言之舜禹稱文明文命而不及武湯稱聖
武而不及文周之謨烈各專其一蓋就其偏而

之術正在是也若夫創業以武守成以文是
蓋各該其要者言之耳如使創業者而無事乎
文則重黎五教書非邪如使守成者
武則五兵張皇六師者非邪慨
===
武令并田疇而兵農判文事簿
書各識其職矣兵執干戈民執耒
耜各事其事矣患兵農之一致文武同方古之
法也不可復於今邪蓋嘗竊譜古矣欽明文思
濬哲文明文命之可數人知之肇脩五教之克
垂堯舜禹湯文武之文德也四凶之誅三苗之
征防風之戮井陑之師牧野之戰堯舜禹湯文
武之武功也彼稱堯之德曰乃武乃文舉其
全而言之舜禹稱文明文命而不及武湯稱聖
武而不及文周之謨烈各專其一蓋統之偏而
punctuated:
義以正天下，故凡選擇將帥、振勵卒伍，干以消折奸宄而為安定之功，皆武之屬也。有武而無文以濟之，則過於義而傷於剛，無以存仁厚之治體；有文而無武以濟之，則過於仁而流於柔，無以立精明之治功。故是二者猶天之二氣，不可相勝；猶車之二輪，不可缺一。陸賈所謂長久之術，其在是也。然所謂創業以武、守成以文，是蓋各就其重者言之耳。如使創業者而無事乎文，則紀綱民物、五教者非邪？如使守成者□□，克詰戎兵、張皇六師者非邪？慨□□□□□□□□武分，井田壞而兵農判，文事簿□□□玩，各職其職矣。兵執干戈，民執耒耜，□乃事其事矣。德兵農一致，文武同方，古之法豈不可復於今邪？

蓋嘗質諸古矣。欽明文思、濬哲文明、文命之敷、人紀之肇脩、五教之克寬，堯舜禹湯文武之文德也。四凶之誅、三苗之征、防風之戮、升陘之師、牧野之戰，堯舜禹湯文武之武功也。彼稱堯之德曰「乃武乃文」，舉其全而言之。舜禹稱文明、文命而不及武，湯稱聖武而不及文，周之謨烈各專其一，蓋就其偏而
translation_en:
…Righteousness rectifies All under Heaven. Thus selecting generals and commanders, invigorating the ranks, and using arms [?] to suppress evildoers and achieve peace and stability all belong to the martial sphere. If martial qualities lack civil qualities to complement them, righteousness becomes excessive and rigidity causes harm, leaving no means to preserve a benevolent and generous foundation of government. If civil qualities lack martial qualities to complement them, benevolence becomes excessive and lapses into weakness, leaving no means to achieve discerning and effective government. These two are therefore like Heaven’s two vital forces: neither should overpower the other. They are like the two wheels of a carriage: neither can be dispensed with. Herein lies what Lu Jia called the art of enduring rule. Yet the saying that one founds a dynasty through martial means and preserves its achievements through civil means merely identifies the greater emphasis in each case. If founders had no need of civil government, would ordering the people and all things and establishing the Five Teachings have been mistaken? If those preserving a dynasty’s achievements [illegible], would putting military forces in order and displaying the might of the Six Armies have been mistaken? Alas, [illegible] the martial sphere became divided [?]; the well-field system collapsed, and soldiers and farmers became separate. Civil affairs [text corrupt and partly illegible] became lax [?], and each attended to his own office. Soldiers held shields and spears; the people held ploughs and ploughshares, [illegible] each attending to his own tasks. [Unclear character] soldiers and farmers united in one system, civil and martial affairs following the same course—could these ancient institutions not be restored today?

I have sought confirmation in antiquity. Reverence, discernment, cultural accomplishment, and thoughtfulness; profound wisdom and civil refinement; the dissemination of civil instruction; the initial ordering of human relationships; and the generous implementation of the Five Teachings: these were the civil virtues of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. The punishment of the Four Malefactors, the campaign against the Sanmiao, the execution of Fangfeng, the expedition to Shengxing [?], and the battle of Muye: these were the martial achievements of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu. The praise of Yao’s virtue as “both martial and civil” speaks of his qualities in their entirety. Shun and Yu are praised for civil refinement and civil instruction, without mention of martial qualities; Tang is praised as sagely and martial, without mention of civil qualities. The plans and achievements of the Zhou kings are each associated exclusively with one of the two. This is presumably speaking from the perspective of one particular aspect…

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
言之爾論者徒見三代迭尚而不言武不知
尚忠尚質尚文之中武備素具矣豈輕於武乎
徒見周列四民而兵不與而不知井邑丘甸同
成之中兵政默寓矣豈忽於兵乎自是而後則

言之爾。論者徒見三代迭尚而不言武，不知尚忠、尚質、尚文之中，武備素具矣，豈輕於武乎？徒見周列四民而兵不與，而不知井邑丘甸同成之中，兵政默寓矣，豈忽於兵乎？自是而後，則有可慨者矣。誅秦興漢，武功已著，而過魯一祀，庶知尚文矣，終不足以蓋輕儒之失。除隋肇唐，武□已振，而弘文一官，庶知尚文矣，終不足以□□德之譏。掃五代□□，建隆之治，武威亦云□□；觀書，文教是崇，而終不足以復帝王□□□。是而遽可許其兼乎文邪？宣室召□□□□□□，庭習射，終莫刷匈奴之恥。延□□□□□不振，而淮蔡甫平，遂以肇驕恣之□□。遺書而入太平之治，政教亦休明矣。河東□，兩浙納土，而終不能復中國之舊。守成若□，遽可許其兼乎武邪？夫櫜鞬是事，而文教□□，削刼除亂之功不足以比湯武；詞章是尚，而武功不競，則致治之美又豈能如成康乎？

論者又謂：「天下安，注意相。」夫任相以治民，道也；然任相而忽將，則緩急何所倚邪？又謂：「天下雖安，忘戰則危。」夫講武以治兵，道也；使恃治而忘亂，則
translation_en:
…they spoke only of one aspect. Commentators see merely that the Three Dynasties successively esteemed different qualities, without mentioning martial affairs. They do not realize that, whether loyalty, simplicity, or cultural refinement was esteemed, military preparations were always in place. How could these dynasties have slighted martial affairs? They see merely that the Zhou classified the people into four occupations without including soldiers. They do not realize that military administration was implicitly embedded in the territorial divisions of jing, yi, qiu, dian, tong, and cheng [?]. How could the Zhou have neglected the military?

After this, however, there is cause for lament. In overthrowing Qin and establishing Han, martial achievement was already manifest. A single sacrifice while passing through Lu suggests an appreciation of civil culture, yet it ultimately could not conceal the fault of slighting Confucian scholars. In eliminating Sui and founding Tang, martial [?] had already flourished. Establishing the Institute for the Advancement of Literature suggests an appreciation of civil culture, yet it ultimately could not overcome the criticism concerning virtue [?]. Sweeping away the Five Dynasties [?], the government of the Jianlong reign could also claim martial might [?]. Reading books and honoring civil instruction nevertheless proved insufficient to restore the [?] of the ancient emperors and kings. Can we therefore readily grant that they also possessed civil accomplishment?

A summons to the Xuanshi Hall [?], and archery practice in the courtyard, ultimately failed to wipe away the humiliation inflicted by the Xiongnu. [?] failed to revive; yet, as soon as Huai and Cai were pacified, this gave rise to arrogance and self-indulgence [?]. The transmitted writings [?] and the advent of peaceful government brought admirable and enlightened administration and instruction. Hedong [?], and the surrender of territory by Liangzhe, nevertheless failed to restore China's former domains. With the preservation of inherited rule being thus [?], can we readily grant that they also possessed martial accomplishment? If bow cases and quivers are one's sole concern while civil instruction [?], achievements in suppressing brigandage and eliminating disorder cannot compare with those of Tang and King Wu. If literary composition is esteemed while martial achievement is weak, how can the excellence of the resulting government equal that of Kings Cheng and Kang?

Commentators also say: “When the realm is at peace, give your attention to the chief minister.” Employing a chief minister to govern the people is indeed the proper way. But if one employs a chief minister while neglecting generals, on whom can one rely in an emergency? They also say: “Even when the realm is at peace, forgetting warfare brings danger.” Practicing martial skills to regulate the armed forces is indeed the proper way. If one relies on good order and forgets disorder, then…

title: 正德六年進士登科錄
text:
安全可常保邪大抵文德敷而後民生遂武功
立而後兵力強缺一則偏缺二則亡御天下之
常道也帝王與後世異者其幾正在於此洪惟
我
太祖高皇帝以武功定天下以文德致太平自今觀
之文取自科貢而銓於吏部武取自閥胄而銓
於兵部其建官有定制矣兵隸於尺伍以供戍
役民編於版圖以輸賦稅其分籍有定制矣而
藩臬諸司於外兵曹維督府於中則文武
又有交修之義率軍士以屯田有警點民壯
===
以協守則兵農又有相通之用良法美意超越近
代固非漢唐之主所能及也故以之垂統而開萬
世之洪基繼自今
聖子神孫史臣贊曰獨禀全智功高千古
列聖相承成
祖宗之成率遵是道督文臣以安民而德化愈洽督
武臣以強兵而功業愈盛但承平久而玩愒生
此又勢之所必至者故學校之法具存而士或失
養育之方無經濟之實而有奔競之風蠲貸之詔屢下
而民或失撫字之恩人多告饑無擊壤之樂而有弄兵之虞則所
謂修文以治民者可慮矣列屯而坐老弱待哺徒

率遵是道督臣以安民而德化愈洽督
以強兵而功業愈盛自承平久而玩偈生
務之所必至者於學校之法具存而士或失
無經濟之實而有奔競之風霸者之憂下
人多告饑無擊壤之樂而有弄兵之虞則所
文以治民者可慮矣列屯而坐老啸徒
punctuated:
安全可常保邪？大抵文德敷而後民生遂，武功立而後兵力強。缺一則偏，缺二則亡，御天下之常道也。帝王與後世異者，其幾正在於此。洪惟我太祖高皇帝以武功定天下，以文德致太平。自今觀之，文取自科貢而銓於吏部，武取自閥胄而銓於兵部，其建官有定制矣；兵隸於尺伍以供戍役，民編於版圖以輸賦稅，其分籍有定制矣。而藩臬諸司於外，兵曹維督府於中，則文武又有交修之義；率軍士以屯田，有警點民壯以協守，則兵農又有相通之用。良法美意，超越近代，固非漢唐之主所能及也。故以之垂統而開萬世之洪基。繼自今，聖子神孫，史臣贊曰：「獨禀全智，功高千古。」列聖相承，成祖宗之成，率遵是道，督文臣以安民而德化愈洽，督武臣以強兵而功業愈盛。

但承平久而玩愒生，此又勢之所必至者。故學校之法具存，而士或失養育之方，無經濟之實而有奔競之風；蠲貸之詔屢下，而民或失撫字之恩，人多告饑，無擊壤之樂而有弄兵之虞，則所謂修文以治民者可慮矣。列屯而坐，老弱待哺，徒
translation_en:
…can safety and security be preserved forever? In general, only when civil virtue is widely extended can the people prosper, and only when military achievements are established can military strength grow. To lack either is to be unbalanced; to lack both is to perish. This is the constant way of governing the realm. The crucial distinction between the ancient sovereigns and rulers of later ages lies precisely here.

We reverently consider how our Emperor Taizu Gao pacified the realm through military achievement and brought about great peace through civil virtue. Viewed from the present, civil officials are recruited through the examinations and tribute-student system and selected for appointment by the Ministry of Personnel; military officials are recruited from hereditary military families and selected for appointment by the Ministry of War. Thus, established regulations govern the creation of official posts. Soldiers are assigned to units [?] to perform garrison service, while the common people are entered in the population and land registers to pay taxes. Thus, established regulations govern their separate registration. With the Provincial Administration Commissions, Provincial Surveillance Commissions, and other offices outside the capital, and the Ministry of War linking the Chief Military Commissions [?] within it, civil and military administration also complement one another. Soldiers are led in cultivating military colonies, and, when an alarm arises, able-bodied civilians are mustered to assist in defense. Thus, military service and agriculture also serve interconnected purposes.

These excellent laws and admirable intentions surpass those of recent ages; they were certainly beyond the reach of the rulers of Han and Tang. Through them, he handed down the succession and laid a vast foundation for ten thousand generations. Henceforth, his sagely sons and divine grandsons—the historian praises him, saying, “He alone possessed complete wisdom; his achievements tower above the ages” [?]—and the successive sage rulers, continuing one another’s work and fulfilling the achievements of their ancestors, have all followed this way. They have directed civil officials to bring peace to the people, making the transforming influence of virtue ever more pervasive; they have directed military officials to strengthen the armed forces, making their achievements ever more flourishing.

Yet prolonged peace produces complacency and heedless delay: this, too, is an inevitable tendency. Thus, although the regulations for schools remain fully in place, scholars sometimes lack proper nurture and training. They lack practical competence in governing, yet display a propensity to scramble for advancement. Although edicts granting tax remissions and loans are repeatedly issued, the people sometimes fail to receive the benevolence of attentive care. Many report hunger; instead of the joy of striking the ground in contentment, there is the danger of taking up arms. What is called cultivating civil governance to govern the people therefore gives cause for concern. Deployed in military colonies, they sit idle; the old and weak await food, merely…

夫文武之道，有不可偏之用，故當求竝用之法。及其久也，無不弊之法，則必當以救弊之人。為今之計，亦惟求其人以行。□□入德之□覃敷者，豈不以司文治之乎？必也慎師儒之選，以正士風；重守，以治其始進也；精科貢之途，以求稱職者有賞，不職者有罰。俟其既□□之典以考之，務使董庠序者如□□，郡邑者如龔遂、如卓茂，則必能□所教，盡循良而民得所養。菁莪□□樸之俗，庶乎可復見矣。
武功，豈不以司武備者之不得其人乎？師之選以通豪俊，謹襲蔭之格以革濫，以正其始進也；嚴□□之法以求之其既仕也，賞其勝任者，罰其不勝任者。俟其既久而後□黜陟之典以考之，務使應募舉者如韓信、如郭子儀，出閥胄者如謝玄、如曹瑋，則必能去冗卒
translation_en:
…merely expending labor on transporting provisions, without showing any success in resisting aggression. When they march in response to a military summons, they live idly at the expense of prefectures and counties: we see only the disruption caused by mobilization, and hear of no achievement in suppressing bandits. Thus what is called ordering the army through military measures gives cause for concern. How could this fail to trouble Your Majesty, who rises before dawn and eats late in attending to affairs?
The civil and military ways have functions neither of which can be neglected; we must therefore seek methods of employing both together. Over time, however, no method is free from abuses, so we must rely on people who can remedy those abuses. The plan for the present is simply to find the right people to carry it out. The passage concerning entry into virtue and its widespread dissemination is damaged [?]; is this not because of those responsible for civil governance [?]? We must carefully select teachers and scholars to rectify the ethos of the educated, and give weight to those charged with guardianship [?], thereby regulating their initial entry into service. We must refine the avenues of recruitment through examinations and tribute recommendation, so as to seek out [suitable men?]. Those who fulfill their duties should be rewarded, and those who do not should be punished. Once they have [text damaged], assess them through the prescribed procedures [?]. Ensure that those who oversee the schools resemble [names illegible], and that those who administer prefectures and counties resemble Gong Sui and Zhuo Mao. Then surely [those taught will receive proper instruction?], all will be conscientious and benevolent, and the people will receive the care they need. The flourishing education evoked by “Luxuriant Mugwort” and the customs of simplicity [intervening text damaged] may perhaps be seen again.
As for military achievement, is the problem not that the right people have not been obtained to oversee military preparedness? [Be careful in?] selecting military leaders so as to open the way for outstanding talent, and strictly observe the rules governing hereditary succession and privilege to eliminate abuses, thereby regulating their initial entry into service. Enforce the [illegible] regulations strictly in seeking out [suitable men?] once they have entered office; reward those who prove capable of their responsibilities and punish those who do not. After they have served for some time, [apply?] the prescribed procedures for dismissal and promotion to assess them. Ensure that those who answer calls for recruitment or are recommended resemble Han Xin and Guo Ziyi, and that those descended from distinguished lineages resemble Xie Xuan and Cao Wei. Then surely it will be possible to eliminate superfluous soldiers…

translation_en:
…[?] may thereby be reduced; bandits and robbers may be suppressed, and the sources of harm to the people removed. The achievement of presenting severed enemy ears at the school by the Pan waters [?] may perhaps be seen again. Thus, fully heeding the warning against idle pleasure, carefully spreading civil virtue throughout the nine [?], and strengthening defense through military achievements [?], those among the Man and Yi who bring disorder to the Chinese realm will subside of themselves, and those who act wantonly will reform of themselves. The ruler [?] will regard the Han, Tang, and Song as inadequate, establish an enduring enterprise, and restore [?]. End of the essay [?].
“You gentlemen aspire to serve the world. On the day of this policy examination, there is no leisure to [?]; I therefore raise only those matters most pressing for the times. Set these forth for me.”
Your foolish servant has fortunately received recommendation through the examinations. The aspiration to serve the world is indeed your foolish servant’s [?]. As for the business of [?] and the matters covered by Your Majesty’s inquiries, I have respectfully set them forth point by point above. In my foolish understanding, there is something pressing for the times that I venture to present: advancing in learning to nourish heavenly virtue. Only diligence can bring about flourishing [?]. [?] Sustain this learning; comprehensively assess all your ministers [?], and the affairs of the realm may be dealt with in sequence [?]. [?] Put this energetically into practice, and in establishing virtue and accomplishing deeds [?], there will naturally be strength to spare for military action. This is what the people hope for as their blessing; how could it be good fortune for your foolish servant alone? [?]…
